newsitem.title: UK: UK minimum wage over 3.5 stg could hit jobs -- study.
newsitem.headline: UK minimum wage over 3.5 stg could hit jobs -- study.

text.p: A minimum wage of 3.50 pounds per hour would not harm British employment, but a wage floor set substantially above this level would inject uncertainty into the jobs market, UK employment think-tank the Employment Policy Institute said on Monday.

"This (a wage floor set at 3.50 pounds) does not rule out setting a higher national minimum wage but a minimum wage set well above this level would take the UK into uncharted and uncertain waters," the Institute said in a study on the wide-ranging impact of implementing a wage floor.

The country's largest trades union UNISON, which represents 1.3 million public sector workers, has told the new Labour government it would like to see a minimum wage of half the median male salary, or 4.42 pounds per hour on updated figures.
UK employer organisations however are concerned that a wage floor set too high could cost thousands of jobs and spark regular strikes over wage levels.

The Employment Policy Institute report reveals a minimum wage of around 3.00 pounds per hour would result in a pay rise of less than 10 percent for those paid less than the minimum, rising to 20 percent or more at 4.00 pounds and above.

"The associated effect on the national wage bill of a national minimum wage set within the 3.00-4.00 pound band would thus range from an increase of around 0.25 percent at 3.00 pounds to over 1.5 percent at 4.00 pounds," the report noted.

Women -- almost half of whom were paid less than 4.00 stg per hour in 1995 -- are likely to benefit disproportionately from a wage floor. As will, more generally, younger workers; those with less education; unskilled workers; people working in firms without unions; or small companies.
Low-paid workers are particularly concentrated in the private sector, especially those in the hotel, retail trade and catering sectors, the report found.
Wider effects of implementing a minimum wage are more difficult to assess or to cost accurately at present, the Institute concluded.
"The impact...on wage costs will extend beyond the direct effect associated with raising pay levels for the low-paid because of wider knock-on effects on pay," it said.

A knock-on impact on wage levels could result if better-paid workers press for the restoration of pay differentials or simply demand a hefty pay rise once those below the floor have enjoyed a hike in their wages, it said.

The Institute urged the Low Pay Commission, the consultative body which will be created to take evidence from employers and workers' representatives before recommending a new minimum wage, to obtain detailed estimates of likely knock-on effects "as a priority".
Together with knock-on wage claims, a wage floor, depending of course on the level at which it is set, is likely to be inflationary.

The report estimates an hourly minimum wage of 3.25 stg accompanied by 25 percent restoration of differentials would increase the inflation rate by 0.6 percent or 1.1 percent for a 3.80 stg minimum wage.

Other issues covered by the report include the possibility of introducing a lower minimum wage to take account of workers on training programmes or so as to allow younger workers to be paid less until they reach a certain age.

The Institute also recommended the level of the minimum wage should be uprated every year but not according to a rigid formula. Any uprating should be made towards the end of the annual pay round, sometime in August in effect.
"...There is a risk that upgrading of the minimum wage will be perceived by wage setters as a benchmark for wage increases across the whole economy," it noted.
